summary: This note covers two parts of Toyota's history. It explains how Toyota's small vehicles were sold under the Toyopet name from September 1947, including the Toyopet SA and several other models, and why the name was dropped for the American market after the 1957 Crown launch. It also describes the US 'chicken tax' of 1964, a 25% tariff on imported light trucks, which led Toyota, Nissan and Honda to build US plants by the early 1980s.
one_line: Toyota's Toyopet brand name history and how the 1964 US 'chicken tax' prompted Japanese automakers to build American plants.
key_facts: From September 1947, Toyota's small-sized vehicles were sold under the name Toyopet (トヨペット).
The first vehicle sold under the Toyopet name was the Toyopet SA.
Other vehicles sold as Toyopet included the Toyopet SB light truck, Toyopet Stout light truck, Toyopet Crown, Toyopet Master, and Toyopet Corona.
The name Toyopet was a nickname given to the Toyota SA due to its small size, resulting from a naming contest the Toyota Company organized in 1947.
When Toyota entered the American market in 1957 with the Crown, the Toyopet name was not well received due to connotations of toys and pets.
The Toyopet name was soon dropped for the American market but continued in other markets until the mid-1960s.
By the early 1960s, the US had begun placing stiff import tariffs on certain vehicles.
The so-called 'chicken tax' of 1964 placed a 25% tax on imported light trucks.
In response to the chicken tax, Toyota, Nissan Motor Co. and Honda Motor Co. began building plants in the US by the early 1980s.
